full_judgment:
13. Mr. Roushan Ali, learned Advocate for the appellant, contends that the finding of the lower appellate Court and the trial Court has been vitiated by an erroneous view of law relating to the presumption of legitimacy as referred to in section 112 of the Evidence Act. The learned Advocate has pointed out that both the trial Court and the lower appellate Court raised the question of paternity of the appellant and entered into the question as to who was appellant's father, whether there was any valid marriage between her alleged mother Gouri Dasi and one Khalipada whom she claimed to be her father and whether she was born of that wed-lock during the subsistence of this marriage. The question of paternity which is the subject matter of section 112 of the Evidence Act is totally irrelevant in this case, the learned Advocate further contends. The learned Advocate also contends that when the defendant-Government has proceeded to take over possession of the suit land asserting that Gouri Dasi died intestate onus of proof lies upon the Government. 

 14. This question has arisen in a suit filed by the appellant for a declaration that she is the owner of the land as Gouri Dasi's daughter and heir. As such, the burden of proof lies upon her alone. Government has of course disputed her claim saying that Gouri Dasi died intestate, without leaving any issue. But defendant-Government is not required to prove anything in this suit, though, in their Misc Case No. 14/75-76 under section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the onus to prove that Gouri Dasi died intestate lies upon the Government. That Misc. Case is not before us nor any order passed therein has been challenged in this suit. Plaintiff-appellant examined three witnesses and filed some documents. She deposed as P.W. 1 claiming that she was born of Gouri Dasi and has been living with her in the suit property which she has been possessing since her mother's death P.W. 2 corroborated her on this point. She (P.W. 2) is another prostitute of the same area, Syedpur, and she categorically stated that the plaintiff is the daughter of Gouri Dasi, who was also a prostitute there. Her evidence has been disbelieved by the Courts below simply on the ground that she did not see the plaintiff being born of Gouri Dasi. In other words, she was not present at the time of plaintiff's birth. But this does not exclude the possibility of her personal knowledge of the fact that the plain-tiff was born of, and was brought up, by Gouri Dasi in the same prostitute area. P.W. 3 has. stated that he knows that plaintiff was Gouri Dasi's daughter; he being a local man is also a competent witness to say whether the plaintiff was Gouri Dasi's daughter. As against this evidence of P.W. 1, 2 and 3, only D.W. 1, Field Kanungo, has come to challenge it; but he is not a member of the locality and has no knowledge about the matter from the time of birth of the plaintiff. An as officer of the Government, he said, he enquired about the matter in the locality and submitted a report that Gouri Dasi died leaving no issue. The enquiry is not found to have been made with notice to the plaintiff; it is not unlikely that interested persons having an eye upon the land misinformed him. Besides the oral evidence, plaintiff produced a certificate from the Chairman-of Syedpur Paurashava (Ext. B) in which it has been stated that the plaintiff, Geeta Rani was Gouri Dasi's daughter. But both the trial Court and the lower appellate Court dismissed this document on the ground that "who was Geeta Ram's father" was not mentioned therein. This shows why the positive evidence adduced by the plaintiff has been rejected by the courts below. 

 15. The question is the maternity of the plaintiff and not her paternity. There is no legal presumption as to maternity. Section 112. of the Evidence Act provides for a legal presumption as to legitimate paternity by saying that if a person is born during the continuance of a valid marriage between his mother and any man or within two hundred and eighty days after its dissolution, then this fact shall be the conclusive proof that he is the legitimate son of that man. This section has no manner of application when the maternal of a person is questioned. The question of maternity—i.e. whether a person is the mother of another person, is purely a question of fact. Plaintiff claimed that Gouri Dasi, though a prostitute at the earlier part of her life, later on married one Kalipada Das and that she was born of that wedlock. But the trial Court. and the lower appellate Court raised the questions whether this marriage is valid or whether there was any such marriage, or who was then the plaintiff's father. These questions are absolutely irrelevant in the present case where the question is whether Gouri Dasi was plaintiff's mother. These Courts proceeded on the erroneous view of law the to prove her maternity, plaintiff is also. required to prove her paternity on the basis of a valid marriage. This totally erroneous view of law is found to have prejudicially influenced the finding that plaintiff was not Gouri Dasi's daughter. This finding is not immune from interference in revision. The evidence adduced by the plaintiff it sufficient to prove her maternity, that is she is Gouri Dasi's daughter and heir.
